book: Warren Buffett and the Interpretation of Financial Statements

1.summary:
Identify a company with a durable competitive advantage.

Value a company with a durable competitive advantage.

2.summary: DCA companies make the most money over the longer term

3.summary:
- A company that sells a unique product/service.
(product eg. Coca-Cola, Pepsi, Hershey's, Budweiser, Coors, Kraft, Waahington post, Proctor & Gamble, Philip Morris)
(service eg. Moody's, H & R Block Inc. AMEX, Service Master Co., Wells Fargo - Institution specific, not people specific)

- Low cost buyer/seller of product/service the public consistently needs. Big margins are traded for volume as increase in volume makes up for low margins. The best price in town becomes part of the consumer's story of where to shop.
(eg. Wal-Mart, Costco, Nebraska, Furniture Mart, Borsheim Jewelers, Burlington Northern, Santa Fe Railway

4.summary:
-Durability creates wealth
(Coca-Cola has been selling the same thing for well over a century)

-Consistency in the product creates consistency in the companies profits.

-The company doesn't have to spend millions to keep changing the product with R&D nor on re-tooling for the next product. Less debt means less interest meaning more money to expand or buy back stock, driving up earnings and the price of the stock.

-Is it consistent? - High gross margin, little to no debt, not spending heavy on R&D?

-All of this info can be found in Financial Statements

5.summary:
Income Statement - How much is earned in a set period? Determines margins - Return equity, cosistency and direction of earnings, these thing determins DSA status.

Balance Sheet - How much is in the bank? How much it owes? Subtract these and you get net worth. Amount of cash and long term debt are indicators of DCA.

Cash Flow Statement - Cash that flows in and out. Good to see how much is spent of capital improvements. Tracks bond/stock sales & repurchases.

6.summary: Warren uses MSN, Yahoo, SEC, Bloomberg

7.summary:
Warren starts with the income statement.

Expenses, Revenue, Profit/Loss

Indicates DSA or Mediocre where the latter shows a struggle year to year in a competitive market.

8.summary:
-Amount of money that comes in in a set period

-Big revenue doesn't mean profitable

-Revenue without expenses means nothing

-After revenue, take a long careul look at the expenses

9.summary:
-AKA the cost of revenue

-The lower the better

-Find out what is included in the cost. It gives a good idea of how management is thinking about the business.

-As a lone number it doesn't tell us much about DSA.

-Determines gross profit

10.summary:
GP Margin = GP / Revenue
eg. 7000 / 10000 = 70%

GP = Revenue - cost of raw good  and labor to make the goods

Doesn't include sales & admin costs, depreciation, interest costs of running the business

GP doesn't tell us much but GP margin can tell us a lot about the economic nature of a business

Consistently higher GP Margins show excellent long term economics working in their favour than those that don't
(eg. Coca-Cola shows 60% + consistently, Moody's 73%, Burlington Northern Santa Fe Railway 61%, Wrigely & Co. 51%)
(Contrast eg. United Airlines 14% and always in & out of bankruptcy, GM 21%, US Steel 17% Goodyear 20% in a bad economy)

Warren stays away from technology because he says he doesn't understand it.
Microsoft 79%
Apple 33%
Indicates that Microsoft has better economics?

DCA creates higher margins hence allows the freedom to price the products/services well in excess of cost of goods sold.

40%+ tend to have DCA but there are exceptions

Lower than 40% indicates a highly competitive industry where competition hurts margins but there are exceptions

Below 20% indicates fiercely competitive industry

Companies without a competitve advantage are never going to make use rich

The GP Margin test is not failsafe but it is an early indicator that they have DCA

Track the last 10 years to ensure consistency as consistency is the name of the game

high research costs, high sellin & admin costs and high interest on debt can strip the competitive advantage potential from a high GP margin company. They can be a thorn in the side of any company. These are called operating expenses

11.summary:
A group of expenses, when added, make up the total operating expenses.

These are all the company's hard costs associated with research and development of new products, selling and administrative costs of getting the product to market, depreciation and amortization, restructuring and impairment charges, and the catch-all "other" that includes all non-operating, non-recurring expenses.

12.summary:
SGA = Selling, General, and Administrative Expenses

Includes management salaries, advertising, travel costs, legal fees, commissions, all payroll costs, etc.

SGA needs to be consistent

If a company cant cut SGA costs fast, these costs eat more of the gross profit

Lower SGA & consistency is key to DCA

Ratio of SGA to GP of 30% and below is great

Coca-Cola average 59%
Moody's average 25%
Proctor & Gamble average 61%

GM 28% to 83% in 5 years

Ford 89% to 780% in 5 years - losing money like crazy

There are many great companies in the 30% to 80% range with DCA

clsoe to and above 100% indicates a highly competitive industry where nobody has a sustainable competivie advantage.

Low to medium SGA with high R&D costs, Capital expenditure or interest expenses on debt still have the same problems as a high SGA company eg. Intel and Goodyear.

Goodyear 72% SGA with high Cap ex & interest from debt to fund the cap ex, but if it didnt add the debt to fund the cap ex, they wouldn't stay comepetitive for very long

13.summary:
If DCA comes from tech advancement, there is always a threat that newer tech will replace it. Eg. Microsoft is afraid of the technological advancements of Google and vice versa as today's competitive advantage may become tomorrow's obsolescence. 

If a competitive advantage is protected by a patent, such as pharmaceuticals, at some point the patent will expire and the competitive advantage will disappear.

These companies that need to continue spending on R&D and invent new products usually must also redesign and update sales programs which means high SGA spending as a consequence.

Merck & Co must spend 29% of its GP on R&D and 49% of its GP on SGA which, when combines, totals 78% of its GP. If it fails to invent. the next multimillion-dollar-selling drug, it loses its competitive advantage when its patents expire.

Intel, when it was the leader in it field, spent approx 30% of its GP on R&D. If it didn't it would lose its competitive advantage in a few years.

There is no worry of losing DCA with Coca-Cola and Moody's, unlike Intel and Merck & Co.

Comapnies that rely headily on R&D have an inherent flaw in their competitive advantage that will put their long term economics at risk which means that they are not a sure thing.

If it's not a sure thing, Warren Buffet is not interested.

14.summary:
All machinery and buildings wear out. This wearing out is shown as depreciation on the balance sheet.

The estimated years from purchase to unusable is divided by the cost. That amount is then accounted for as a cost for each year up to the final year

eg. imagine a printing press is bought by XYZ Printing Corporation for $1,000,000. This printing press has a life span of 10 years. Because it has a lifespan of 10 years the IRS will not let the company expense the press in the year it was purchased. It must be expensed every year over the 10 years that it is in service; at $100,000 per year. This annual $100,000 example is called Depreciation and is a real cost for a business as that press will eventually need to be replaced. The initial $1,000,000 purchase will show up on the balance sheet in the Plant and Equipment asset count. Each year $100,000 will be subtracted from that asset count and be added to the Depreciation cost. The initial $1,000,000 purchase will show up on the cash folw statement as a Capital Expenditure. Remember that the $1,000,000 dollar purchase is NOT allocated as an expense in the year that it was bought. Rather, it is expensed over 10 years as a Depreciation expense every year.

Many Wall Street types regard this as a cost that doesn't cost any real money that yeat, yet it reduces income reported or that year. Wall street types have created an acronym called EBITDA (Earnings Before Income Tax, Depreciation and Amortisation), where they add those numbers back into earnings so that they can use the number to sell the idea that the cash flow of the business can now support more debt for new ventures such as leveraged buyouts. Warren disagrees with this idea and does not look at EBITDA because he feels that, by doing this,  the Wall Street types are ignoring the fact that the printing press will eventually wear out and XYZ may not have the ability to finance another $1,000,000 purchase of a new printing press.

Warren believes that depreciation is a very real expense and should always be included in any calculation of earnings. To do otherwise is delusional as it makes peopl believe that the company is earning more than it actually is.

DCA companies have lower depreciation costs as a percentage of gross profit than companies that have intense competition

Coca-Cola - 6%
Wrigely's & Co - 7%
Proctor & Gamble - 8%

GM - 22% to 57%

According to Warren, like with any expense, les is alway more, as more eats into a company's profit
